newsitem.title: USA: Levi's Slates is the latest sibling going retail.
newsitem.headline: Levi's Slates is the latest sibling going retail.

text.p: It's the newest and maybe the oldest ploy in the grand game of American consumer marketing. Start a second brand-name to enter another market niche, gain more retail exposure and so carve out another avenue for profits.
There's built-in risk, of course. The new brand may just cannibalize the old one if the marketer becomes careless.

The latest entry into big-scale, new-brand marketing is Levi Strauss, the world's largest apparel producer. A few weeks ago, the giant San Francisco producer introduced Slates, a new, upscale brand of men's dress pants, into some 1,500 department stores.

For Levi, whose Levi jeans are already an American icon and whose Dockers casual pants have become an industry standout, the $50 to $80 Slates are only the third major brand launched in the company's 140-year history.

Flush with 1995 sales of $6.7 billion, Levi Strauss says it expects the new brand to eventually hit $1 billion in sales and is spending more than $20 million this fall alone to start the ball rolling.

Why did Levi launch a third brand? "Our focus groups of male baby boomers told us that many wanted to look professional and yet keep their own individual styles in clothes," said Cassie Ederer, senior marketing specialist at Levi Strauss.

"They wanted sophisticated clothing that's comfortable, expressive and affordable. We call it 'accessible style,' dress pants styled between suits and cotton pants," she added. "Much like designer pants, but at a substantially lower price...for either for business and social occasions."

The loose, draped Slates pants come in a broad range of styles and fabrics including all-cotton, all cotton-gabardine and various blends and with flat fronts and single, double and inverted box pleats. Almost all have pre-sized waists and lengths, so that no tailoring is needed.
Their pricing puts them at the high level for Levi products, $50 to $80 versus the roughly $30 to $40 for Dockers and $18 to $30 for Levi jeans.

Using Foote, Cone & Belding's San Francisco office as its advertising agency, Levi has been running three types of 30-second television spots with the blurb, "These Are Those Pants," aimed at 34- to 49-old males.

The spots, entitled "Tango," "Hotel" and "Rush Hour", present lightly humorous scenes in which the man demonstrates his individualistic, slightly befuddled manner with his new Slates pants in effect helping him come through as hero.

Slates is part of a reinvigorated trend toward brand names as more vital in marketing than mass advertising, says Sam Hill, vice president and chief marketing officer at Booz, Allen & Hamilton, the large marketing consulting company.

"In this world of fragmentation, cacophony of noise and jaded consumers, the public seems to be more interested in distinctive names and products that it can relate to," Hill says, "like 'Airwalks,' put out by Airwalk Shoes, which are all the rage among teenage boys for tennis shoes."
But he cautioned that a new brand started by an already successful brand marketer "can be stretched too far. A brand establishes a close bond between the producer and public."

Allan Gardner, managing partner for corporate communications at New York advertising agency Bozell Worldwide, the 1980's witnessed a widespread "milking of brands. Too many marketers took a healthy brand and slapped its name on a bunch of other products to extend the shelf space they got."
Levi, however, has "the power to create a halo for other brands such as Dockers. Levi is on the short list of the world's greatest brands.'

But how a product will perform in the market is difficult to gauge. Jim Spaeth, president of the Advertising Research Foundation in New York, questioned whether Levi had undertaken any test-marketing of the brand before its launch. "Too many fashion businesses are driven by judgment, not adequate research," he said.

The Slates brand was not test-marketed, said Kerri Chessen Lehman, vice president and management supervisor of Levi ad agency Foote Cone Belding, "but we did a lot of qualitative research with consumer focus groups."
"We think that Slates has the potential for global expansion and for its own line extension into other products, too," Chessen said.
